```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                     fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
library(offlineatlas)
```

## What you will make

This tutorial creates a GDP map, a Florence marriage network, and an FDI
map that changes over time. You will customize the controls and legend from
R, export independent HTML files, and make an editable static figure.

For a **living example**, visit [FDI Atlas](https://fdiatlas.engagedthinking.com/),
Keith A. Preble's interactive website for exploring foreign direct investment.
That earlier project helped shape offlineatlas. This tutorial builds smaller,
standalone examples of related mapping and network workflows.

Publishing an offlineatlas map can be as simple as uploading the generated
`.html` file to your website and linking to it. Visitors can explore the map
in their browsers without a running R session or a Shiny server. They can
also download that same file and open it offline.

FDI Atlas uses a more elaborate hosting arrangement, including a dataset
stored in a private folder. The offlineatlas examples here embed their mapped
data in the HTML itself, so those data are included whenever you share the file.

Visiting the hosted FDI Atlas requires an internet connection. The link is
optional; this tutorial and its exported maps work offline.

R prepares the data and writes the files. The exported viewers contain their
data, geometry, JavaScript and CSS. People opening them need only a browser.
They do not need R, Shiny, a server, an API key or an internet connection.
Copying the HTML file alone is enough. The viewer never retrieves new data;
rebuild it in R when you want to update the underlying observations.

The package API is experimental. This tutorial uses bundled snapshots and
does not download data. sf handles geographic inputs and ggplot2 creates
static figures. Both are required R dependencies and are installed automatically
when missing during the standard GitHub installation.

```{r install-package, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("preblek/offlineatlas")
```

Installing R packages may require internet access. Systems that build sf from
source may also need system libraries or build tools; see the
[sf installation guide](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/#installing).
These authoring dependencies do not change the offline HTML export.

```{r libraries}
library(offlineatlas)
```

## Choose an output folder

For this tutorial, use a temporary folder so running examples does not write
into your project or the installed package. For files you want to keep,
replace `output_dir` with a folder you own, such as `"my-atlases"`.

```{r output-folder}
output_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "offlineatlas-tutorial")
dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

The examples use `overwrite = TRUE` so you can rerun them in this folder.
The default for `export_html()` is `FALSE`, which protects existing files.

## 1. Map a variable across countries

A choropleth colors geographic areas according to a variable. Here, country
colors represent **GDP per capita in 2024, in current US dollars**. These are
nominal values, not purchasing-power-adjusted values.

Read the bundled boundaries and GDP snapshot. Join by a stable country ID,
not by row order or the spelling of a country name. `match()` returns `NA`
for an unmatched ID. Keep those rows so their boundaries remain on the map.

```{r gdp-data}
world <- sf::st_read(example_file("world_sf.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)
gdp <- example_data("worldbank_gdp")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(gdp$id))

joined <- match(world$id, gdp$id)
world$gdp <- gdp$gdp_per_capita[joined]
world$matched <- !is.na(joined)
```

`matched` distinguishes a country without a matching source record from a
matched record whose GDP value is unavailable. Both appear as missing on the
map, but details and data downloads preserve the distinction. No missing
value is replaced with zero.

Start with `atlas()`, then add the geographic data with `add_areas()`. Column
names are quoted strings. `values` selects the variable to color, and `labels`
supplies its reader-facing name.

```{r gdp-map}
gdp_map <- atlas(
  "GDP per capita in 2024",
  units = "USD",
  entity_name = "country", entity_names = "countries",
  notice = "Current US dollars. Missing observations are not imputed.",
  sources = c(
    "World Bank WDI, 2024 snapshot, CC BY 4.0.",
    "Natural Earth boundaries, public domain."
  )
) |>
  add_areas(
    world, id = "id", label = "label",
    values = "gdp", labels = "GDP per capita (USD)",
    matched = "matched",
    breaks = list(c(1000, 5000, 15000, 40000, 80000))
  )

export_html(gdp_map, file.path(output_dir, "gdp.html"), overwrite = TRUE)
```

Five breakpoints create six color intervals. A value exactly on a breakpoint
belongs to the higher interval, so 5,000 belongs to the interval beginning at
5,000. Missing values have their own legend key. The `breaks` argument is a
list because an area map can expose more than one variable.

Open the exported file directly in a browser. In an interactive R session,
you can also use the following command.

```{r open-gdp, eval=FALSE}
utils::browseURL(file.path(output_dir, "gdp.html"))
```

For your own map, use `sf::st_read()` to read local boundaries, join your
variables by identifiers, and pass the resulting `sf` object to `add_areas()`.
Polygon and multipolygon geometry is supported. A valid CRS must be present;
projected inputs are transformed during preparation. The HTML display uses a
fixed equirectangular projection with latitude coverage from -60 to 85.
Invalid shapes and out-of-range geometry produce errors. Repair or clip them
explicitly before mapping. The package does not guess a CRS or silently
remove features.

### Inspect the data before exporting

`summary()` reports what is actually in the atlas. It separates matched
records with missing values from areas with no matching record, and keeps
zero and negative values distinct. The result contains ordinary data frames
that you can inspect or save.

```{r summary-gdp}
audit <- summary(gdp_map)
audit$areas
```

`missing` includes both `unmatched` and `unavailable`, so do not add those
three columns together. For a timeline, `areas` contains one row per variable
and period. `categories` counts every declared category, including unused
ones. `relationships` reports supplied ties by period and layer. Numeric sign
counts are `NA` for categories and unweighted networks. The summary cannot
recover source records that you removed before creating the atlas.

### Frame a region automatically

Call `set_view()` without bounds to fit the supplied geographic data. This
example uses the bundled European boundaries for Belgium, the Netherlands
and Luxembourg. Its values are joined from the same GDP snapshot.

```{r automatic-region}
europe <- sf::st_read(example_file("europe_sf.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)
region <- europe[europe$id %in% c("BEL", "NLD", "LUX"), ]
joined <- match(region$id, gdp$id)
region$gdp <- gdp$gdp_per_capita[joined]
region$matched <- !is.na(joined)
regional_map <- atlas(
  "GDP per capita in the Benelux countries", units = "USD",
  sources = "World Bank WDI, 2024 (CC BY 4.0); Natural Earth (public domain)."
) |>
  add_areas(region, label = "label", values = "gdp", matched = "matched",
            breaks = list(c(40000, 80000))) |>
  set_view(title = "Benelux", padding = 0.05) |>
  set_preset("compact")
export_html(regional_map, file.path(output_dir, "regional-gdp.html"),
            overwrite = TRUE)
```

Add all geographic layers before fitting. The function includes every
supplied feature, even if its value is missing. It preserves islands and
outlying territories, so subset the geometry explicitly when you want only
a particular region. It does not change projection. Very small regions have
a minimum one-degree span; dateline-crossing geometry can require a world
view. Prepared SVG path tables still need explicit bounds.

## 2. Draw the Florence marriage network

Networks use a table of entities and a table of relationships. Node IDs must
be unique. Both endpoints of each relationship must match a node ID.

The Florence fixture includes marriage and business relationships. Select
only marriage ties for this example. Family positions are a supplied
schematic layout, not historical residential locations.

```{r florence-data}
families <- example_data("florence_nodes")
ties <- example_data("florence_edges")
marriages <- ties[ties$layer == "Marriage", ]
stopifnot(nrow(marriages) > 0)
```

```{r florence-map}
marriage_map <- atlas(
  "Marriage alliances in Florence",
  entity_name = "family", entity_names = "families",
  notice = paste(
    "Teaching subset. Positions show network structure,",
    "not historical residences."
  ),
  sources = c(
    "Padgett / CoMuNe Lab Florentine families data.",
    "Database ODbL 1.0; individual contents DbCL 1.0.",
    "https://github.com/CoMuNeLab/Padgett-Florentine-Families",
    "https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1-0/",
    "https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/dbcl/1-0/",
    "Expanded family names and rescaled supplied schematic coordinates."
  )
) |>
  add_nodes(
    families, id = "id", label = "label",
    layout_x = "x", layout_y = "y", coordinates = "schematic"
  ) |>
  add_edges(
    marriages, from = "from", to = "to", layer = "layer",
    directed = FALSE, coverage = "edge_list"
  )

export_html(marriage_map, file.path(output_dir, "florence.html"),
            overwrite = TRUE)
```

Read the full source and license notice with
`readLines(example_file("FLORENCE-NOTICE.txt"))`. Keep those notices when
redistributing the data. This example is a teaching subset, not the complete
network from the original study.

To compare marriage and business layers, supply `ties` instead of `marriages`
in a **new** atlas construction. Nodes, relationships and areas can each be
added once. There is no automatic graph layout; supply schematic coordinates
or geographic locations. For geographic networks, `add_nodes()` accepts
longitude and latitude columns or `sf` POINT geometry.

For weighted flows, use `weight` with `coverage = "observed_rows"`, or a
complete directed panel with `coverage = "complete_panel"` and a time column.
An omitted observed row is not assumed to be zero. Negative weights require
`signed = TRUE`. The `add_edges()` help page explains the coverage contract.

## 3. Add an FDI timeline

A numeric area timeline has one row per country and period. Every period
must have the same IDs, labels and geometry. Values, matching status and
notes can change. Include explicit `NA` observations for missing values.

Use the bundled national inward FDI snapshot for 1990-2025. Units are millions
of current US dollars. Negative flows, reported zeroes and unavailable values
remain distinct. The separate bilateral FDI fixture is not used here, and
its sample flows must not be treated as national totals.

These UNCTAD Data Hub data use CC BY 3.0 IGO. Read
`readLines(example_file("FDI-NOTICE.txt"))` for the source and adaptations, and
retain attribution and the license link in shared outputs. The
[Data Hub reuse terms](https://unctadstat.unctad.org/EN/About.html) apply to
these data separately from the package's MIT software license.

```{r fdi-panel}
# Start with a fresh boundary table, without the GDP attributes.
boundaries <- sf::st_read(example_file("world_sf.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)
fdi <- example_data("fdi_national")
periods <- sort(unique(fdi$year))

frames <- lapply(periods, function(period) {
  records <- fdi[fdi$year == period, ]
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(records$id[nzchar(records$id)]))
  joined <- match(boundaries$id, records$id)
  frame <- boundaries
  frame$year <- period
  frame$matched <- !is.na(joined)
  frame$inflow <- records$inflow_usd_millions[joined]

  # Preserve missing-data reasons and source footnotes in each period.
  frame$note <- vapply(joined, function(j) {
    if (is.na(j)) return("No matching source record for this area and year.")
    parts <- c(records$inflow_usd_millions_missing_reason[j],
               records$inflow_usd_millions_footnote[j])
    paste(parts[!is.na(parts) & nzchar(parts)], collapse = ". ")
  }, character(1))
  frame
})
observations <- do.call(rbind, frames)
```

Creating each frame from the same boundary table preserves the complete
roster and fixed geometry. Countries without records stay in the panel with
`NA` values. Historical economy identifiers are not reassigned to successors.

```{r fdi-map}
fdi_map <- atlas(
  "FDI inflows over time", units = "USD millions",
  entity_name = "country or area", entity_names = "countries and areas",
  notice = paste(
    "Annual inward flows, current USD millions. Negative values and zeroes",
    "are retained. Present-day boundaries are used in every period;",
    "historical economies are not reassigned. Revision status is not supplied."
  ),
  sources = c(
    "UNCTAD Data Hub, FDI flows and stock. CC BY 3.0 IGO.",
    "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/igo/",
    "National inward flows, 1990-2025; regional aggregates excluded.",
    "Natural Earth boundaries, public domain. No UN endorsement is implied."
  )
) |>
  add_areas(
    observations, id = "id", label = "label",
    values = "inflow", labels = "FDI inflows (USD millions)",
    time = "year", matched = "matched", notes = "note",
    breaks = list(c(-10000, 0, 1000, 10000, 100000)),
    colors = list(c("#a9602d", "#e4b87e", "#edf4db",
                    "#8fc1a0", "#247577", "#164c60"))
  ) |>
  set_controls(initial_time = "2025")

export_html(fdi_map, file.path(output_dir, "fdi-timeline.html"),
            overwrite = TRUE)
```

Open the file, choose a year, or use Previous, Play and Next. Color intervals
stay fixed across years. Playback advances between supplied observations at
equal intervals, without interpolation. Select exactly one country to reveal
its numeric history chart and table. Missing values break the line; zero and
negative observations remain visible. The history scale stays fixed for the
selected country across playback, but can differ between countries.

The same panel structure supports categorical timelines such as EU
enlargement. Supply `categories = list(levels)` and an explicit color vector
through `colors`, with `time = "year"`. Categorical colors retain their meaning
throughout the series. Categorical variables do not produce a numeric history
chart. The installed `examples/eu.R` script contains the full enlargement
example, using present-day boundaries and documented membership dates.

## 4. Customize controls, legends and fonts

Start with a reusable preset when you want coordinated defaults.
`compact` uses smaller legend keys and tighter spacing; `presentation` uses
larger text and keys. Both use local sans-serif fonts and preserve data,
labels, source notes, initial filters and control visibility.

```{r presets}
compact_map <- set_preset(fdi_map, "compact")
presentation_map <- set_preset(fdi_map, "presentation")
```

Presets set layout fields, including toolbar position, legend placement and
fonts. Use them before your own overrides. Static legends choose a column
count based on category count and label length unless you set one explicitly.
You still choose figure width and height when saving with ggplot2.

You can make presentation changes in R without editing JavaScript or CSS.
Here, keep the initial year explicit, move the toolbar, slow playback, and
provide readable labels for the six fixed FDI intervals.

```{r customize}
custom_map <- fdi_map |>
  set_controls(
    initial_time = "2025", position = "above_map", playback_interval = 1800,
    visible = c(search = TRUE, downloads = TRUE),
    labels = c(play = "Animate", pause = "Pause", "next" = "Later")
  ) |>
  set_legend(
    title = "Annual inward FDI", position = "below", columns = 2,
    missing_label = "Unavailable or unmatched",
    labels = list(inflow = c(
      "<-10,000", "-10,000 to <0", "0 to <1,000",
      "1,000 to <10,000", "10,000 to <100,000", "\u2265100,000"
    ))
  ) |>
  set_style(font_family = "sans", heading_family = "sans")

export_html(custom_map, file.path(output_dir, "fdi-customized.html"),
            overwrite = TRUE)
```

Legend aliases change display text only. Original values remain in data
exports. Labels are plain text. Fonts come from the viewing computer and are
not downloaded, so exact appearance may vary.

Each configuration function replaces its own previous settings with its
arguments and defaults. Keep the desired options together in one call.
For example, when changing playback speed, repeat `initial_time` if you want
to retain a previously configured starting period. A control appears only
when relevant to the supplied data, even if requested as visible. Hiding
controls does not remove data from the HTML.

To start on Europe, use `set_view(custom_map, c(-25, 33, 45, 72))`.
To add one separate detail panel, use
`set_inset(custom_map, c(-15, 34, 35, 62), title = "Europe detail")`.
Bounds are west, south, east and north. Both functions return an updated
atlas, so assign the result before exporting. Regional framing does not
change the map projection, and dateline-crossing bounds are unsupported.

## 5. Make a static figure with ggplot2

An atlas built from `sf` polygons can also become an ordinary ggplot object.
Choose an original variable column name and, for a timeline, one period.
The static map preserves interval boundaries, colors, missing values and
legend aliases. Add normal ggplot2 themes, labels or layers afterwards.

```{r static-figure}
p <- as_ggplot(set_preset(custom_map, "compact"),
               variable = "inflow", time = 2025) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "FDI inflows in 2025",
    subtitle = "Millions of current US dollars"
  ) +
  ggplot2::guides(fill = ggplot2::guide_legend(
    title = NULL, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE
  )) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 8),
    legend.key.size = grid::unit(3, "mm")
  )
# Wrap the retained source caption to fit this figure's width.
p <- p + ggplot2::labs(
  caption = paste(strwrap(p$labels$caption, width = 80), collapse = "\n")
)
p
ggplot2::ggsave(file.path(output_dir, "fdi-2025.png"), p,
                width = 9, height = 5.3, dpi = 150)
```

The static legend is adjustable. `guide_legend(ncol = 4)` makes two compact
rows for these seven keys. `legend.text` sets label size and `legend.key.size`
sets swatch size. `guide_legend(title = NULL)` removes the redundant legend title;
the subtitle already gives the units. Use `legend.position = "right"` to
move the legend, or `"none"` to hide it. These ggplot2 changes apply to this
static figure without changing the interactive atlas.

An interval labeled `0 to <1,000` includes zero and values such as 999.5,
but excludes 1,000. The highest interval uses the greater-than-or-equal symbol.

Static output supports area maps. It does not reproduce network plots,
browser selection, history charts or the browser's current zoom. Visible
insets are omitted with a warning. Build the atlas from `sf` input if you want
static output; prepared SVG path tables do not retain the required geometry.

## Share and inspect the results

The five HTML files can be opened directly and shared independently. The
example code below lists them without launching a browser during a build.
Temporary files may be removed when your R session ends. Copy the files you
want to keep to a permanent folder.

```{r check-outputs, include=FALSE}
expected <- c("florence.html", "gdp.html", "fdi-timeline.html",
              "fdi-customized.html", "regional-gdp.html")
stopifnot(all(file.exists(file.path(output_dir, expected))))
```

```{r list-outputs}
list.files(output_dir, pattern = "[.]html$")
```

The viewer offers several downloads.

- **SVG and PNG** capture the visible map or network, with its captions,
  legend and any visible inset or numeric history chart.
- **View data CSV** follows the current filters and selection.
- **History CSV** contains every period for the selected country.
- **All data JSON** retains all embedded periods and mapped data, regardless
  of hidden controls. It retains original prepared node coordinates.

Search narrows the selection list, not the underlying map data. Clear focus
restores all entities while retaining filters and zoom. Exporting a current
view pauses playback. CSV text that could be interpreted as a spreadsheet
formula receives a protective apostrophe; JSON preserves the original text.

For the complete API, use `help(package = "offlineatlas")` and the individual
function pages, especially `?add_areas`, `?add_edges`, `?set_controls` and
`?export_html`. The package overview is available with `?offlineatlas`.
